1. Mucosal Immunity Background and Celiac Disease

How to use thisDr. Nash (microbiologist) covers pathogenesis, symptom-to-diagnosis reasoning and characteristics of nine immune-related GI disorders. His slides have no red; his "Some Main Points" slides are treated as highest yield. His four end-of-lecture practice cases appear in the last section.

Mucosal immunity

  • M cells sample luminal antigen; beneath them is a Peyer's patch (dendritic cells, B cells, T cells, macrophages).
  • The mucosa is finely balanced between tolerance and response: tolerance to normal flora and food; inflammation is more limited than elsewhere; intact epithelium with tight junctions.
  • Secretory IgA is specific to the mucosa: dimeric IgA binds receptors on epithelium, is transported across, and gets a secretory chain.
  • GI immune diseases most commonly involve Th1, Th17 and CTL.

Celiac disease

  • Hypersensitivity to gluten (gliadin); type IV hypersensitivity: mainly Th1 (CD4) cells, with CTL also involved. Villi are damaged to flattening (essentially absent in most patients).
  • Symptoms (vary): diarrhea, bloating, gas, fatigue, weight loss, iron-deficiency anemia, constipation, depression, itchy rash. Weight loss and nutritional deficiencies come from reduced villous surface area. Many have mild, unrecognized disease.
Normal vs celiac jejunum (slide 7) (click to enlarge)

Pathogenesis

  1. Tissue transglutaminase (tTG) converts glutamine → glutamic acid (deamidation) at motifs such as QXXF and QXPF found in gliadin, creating a new epitope that binds MHC differently.
  2. Strong association with class II MHC HLA-DQ2 and DQ8: nearly necessary (very low risk without them), but not sufficient.
  3. Gliadin is phagocytosed by an APC, presented on class II MHC to CD4 T cells → inflammatory cytokines → villous damage over time.
  4. Intraepithelial lymphocytes (CD8 CTL and NK cells; epithelium expresses only class I MHC, so CD4 cells are not IELs): epithelium modified by gluten expresses stress/damage markers bound by alternate receptors on CD8/NK cells → apoptosis of epithelial cells, flattening villi. The CD4 cells (main player) probably induce the markers.
Tissue transglutaminase deamidation (slide 16) (click to enlarge)

Diagnosis

  • Best would be gluten-specific T cells (too cumbersome). Anti-tTG levels correlate with villous atrophy (Marsh score); antibodies are a side effect (not pathogenic) but diagnostic.
  • Anti-tTG IgA: sensitive and specific. Anti-tTG IgG: check for IgA deficiency if IgG present. Others: anti-endomysium (IgA), anti-gliadin (IgA and IgG), anti-deamidated gliadin.
  • Initial screening: antibodies ± genetics (HLA-DQ2/DQ8), then endoscopy ± biopsy = most definitive diagnosis.
  • Celiac and Crohn's share genetic risk loci.
Transglutaminase index rises with villous atrophy (slide 25) (click to enlarge)
Endoscopy and histology: celiac vs gluten-free (slide 24) (click to enlarge)

2. Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Crohn Disease and Ulcerative Colitis

Pain location: lecture inconsistencyHis comparison table (slide 35) says Crohn pain is commonly lower right and UC pain lower left. His narration and summary slide say the opposite (Crohn left, UC right). The table matches standard teaching; know both if asked.
  • Both are type IV hypersensitivities with abnormal inflammation: tolerance and tempering break down.
  • Immunologic abnormalities: defective defensin expression (innate); inadequate negative regulation to commensals; overactive Th17 response; granulomatous inflammation by IFN-γ-producing Th1 cells; defective autophagy; decreased Tregs (number ± function).
  • Barrier-defect model: mucosal barrier breakdown (loosened tight junctions) lets bacterial antigens reach dendritic cells and macrophages, activating Th1 and Th17 cells (cause not explained).
IBD barrier-defect pathogenesis model (slide 38) (click to enlarge)
Crohn vs ulcerative colitis comparison (slide 35) (click to enlarge)
Crohn diseaseUlcerative colitis
DistributionAnywhere in the GI tract; patchy ("skip"); most often terminal ileum; entire thickness of the wallLarge bowel only; contiguous; mucosa only
Wall / ulcersWall thickened, cobblestone mucosa, deep ulcers (all layers), abscessesWall thinner; shallow ulcers not beyond inner lining; pseudopolyps
ImmunologyTh17 (IL-17) a major contributor; granulomas; stricture (narrowed lumen)Crypt abscesses with neutrophils; Paneth cell defensin defect
OtherFever, malabsorption/malnutrition, weight loss; mouth, eyes, skin involvement (T cells migrate)Rectal bleeding with bowel movements (not common in Crohn)

Crohn disease stages (theory)

  1. Epithelial barrier breakdown lets antigens into the submucosa. 2. Antigens are not cleared; innate inflammation. 3. T cells activate and form granulomas (a continuing antigen source), adaptive inflammation and narrowing.
Phases of Crohn disease (slide 41) (click to enlarge)

Ulcerative colitis crypt abscesses

  • In the crypts there is little luminal movement, so bacteria and antigens linger; the inflammatory response recruits neutrophils, some of which enter the crypt lumen and stay, forming crypt abscesses that can close off into pockets of constant immune stimulation.
  • Possible contributor: defective defensin production by Paneth cells at the crypt base.
Neutrophil accumulation in UC crypts (slide 49) (click to enlarge)

Diagnosis and treatment

  • T-cell testing ideal but impractical: history, genetics, blood tests (symptom/antibody correlates), colonoscopy. Tests trade sensitivity vs specificity; pairs do better (e.g., capsule endoscopy + colonoscopy/ileoscopy: 100% sensitivity but 57% specificity; a pair with 100% specificity misses ~1 in 5 patients).
  • Treatment is limited, mostly reducing the immune response (side effects). Experimental: deliberate helminth infection (hookworm, whipworm) to boost Th2, which suppresses Th1 (and probably Th17); results inconsistent.

3. Cholangitis: PSC, PBC and IgG4-Related Sclerosing Cholangitis

Cholangitis = inflammation of the bile ducts. None has clear pathogenesis; all can progress to cirrhosis and liver failure (damage from bile backing up as ducts are destroyed).

PSC vs PBC (slide 55) (click to enlarge)
Primary sclerosing (PSC)Primary biliary (PBC)IgG4-related sclerosing
DuctsIntrahepatic and extrahepaticIntrahepatic onlyBile ducts, but disease is multi-organ (often pancreas)
MechanismProbably response to bacterial antigens from the gut: bacteria enter the common bile duct (blockage may contribute); T cells and antibodies; complement activation and CD4 cytokinesHypothesized autoimmune (target unclear); chronic inflammationIdiopathic; high IgG4 (possibly result, not cause); B cells and Tfh cytokines at site; MHC allele correlation suggests T-cell epitopes
Imaging image"Beads on a string"Small duct damage—

Why IgG4 is odd

  • It can swap Fab arms and become bivalent for two different epitopes (functionally monovalent for each).
  • Its Fc does not bind NK-cell Fc receptors (no killing), phagocyte Fc receptors (no opsonization) and does not fix complement; poor cross-linking (little agglutination/precipitation). It mostly blocks/neutralizes and tempers responses.
  • Mouse study: ovalbumin-expressing islets + ovalbumin-specific CTL and IgG4 gave inflammation driven by follicular helper T cells, suggesting IgG4 can contribute.
IgG4 characteristics (slide 62) (click to enlarge)

4. Autoimmune Pancreatitis, Food Allergies and IgA Deficiency

Autoimmune pancreatitis

  • Type 1 = IgG4-related disease (part of the multi-organ syndrome, often with cholangitis). Type 2 = other autoimmunity (typical immune mediators: T cells, mast cells, etc.). Both idiopathic. May be a type IV hypersensitivity, probably oversimplified.

Food allergies

  • Mostly type I hypersensitivity (IgE); some type IV (celiac); some mixed. Allergy ≠ intolerance (lactose intolerance is not a milk allergy).
  • Common foods vary; all can cause anaphylaxis; peanuts are notoriously dangerous.
TypeMechanism / features
IgE-mediatedFood-specific IgE on mast cells; allergen cross-links → degranulation (histamine); acute or chronic cutaneous symptoms or anaphylaxis; most prevalent in young children
Non-IgE (Th2-mediated)Chronic skin and/or GI symptoms; eosinophilic disorders
MixedBoth
  • Degranulation requires: IgE already made, allergen present, and mast cells bearing that IgE.
  • Symptoms: vomiting and diarrhea (fluid into lumen), urticaria (hives)/rash, respiratory effects, itchy eyes, anaphylaxis if systemic. Hives are a key clue for type I.
Start of a type I hypersensitivity (slide 78) (click to enlarge)
  1. Antigen reaches the immune system (M cell → Peyer's patch, leak through loosened tight junctions, or during absorption). 2. Dendritic cell presents on class II MHC. 3. If the milieu favors Th2, Th2 cells signal B cells to make IgE. 4. IgE binds mast cells: the person is now allergic.

Selective IgA deficiency

  • Most common primary immunodeficiency; genetic; little or no IgA; majority asymptomatic (IgM and IgG compensate), so underdiagnosed.
  • If symptomatic: more mucosal infections (respiratory, GI, reproductive); no unusual diseases.
  • Link to celiac testing: anti-tTG IgG suggests IgA deficiency.
Selective IgA deficiency (slide 79) (click to enlarge)

5. His Practice Cases and Disease Comparison

A. 27-year-old man: fatigue, dark urine, dull abdominal pain, jaundice; ↑ALP; ducts inside AND outside the liver; no pancreatic involvement.Primary sclerosing cholangitis. IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis is similar but more often involves the pancreas; PBC involves intrahepatic ducts only (his key sentence says PBC 'does not involve intrahepatic ducts,' which is a slip); autoimmune pancreatitis and oyster allergy do not cause liver damage.
B. 56-year-old woman: acute vomiting and diarrhea, red patches (urticaria) on cheek and tongue, no prior episodes.Type I hypersensitivity. Urticaria is the clue; she may have made IgE at a prior exposure.
C. 37-year-old woman: chronic abdominal distress, left-sided pain, malnutrition; biopsy shows thickened wall with deep ulcers.Crohn disease. Thickened wall and deep ulcers.
D. 55-year-old man with celiac disease: most characteristic?Development of anti-transglutaminase (not always present, but characteristic). Low BP = type I; extrahepatic duct inflammation = PSC (his key says PBC, a slip); separated patches with shallow ulcers = mixing up UC/Crohn features; mucosal infections = IgA deficiency.

PBCAutoimmuneIntrahepatic ducts only
IgG4-SC / type 1 AIPIdiopathic; high IgG4; MHC associationMulti-organ; pancreas
